_export_meta.adaptation_notes: BTEC Component 3 introduces the WHO definition of health early. This spec specifies four named definitions (health, illness, disease, well-being) with three distinct authoritative sources (WHO, BMJ, Psychology Today) which must be reproduced. Reuse the WHO definition pattern; rebuild the other three from spec. Add the 'holistic, varies across culture/time/life stages' interpretive layer that is unique to this qualification.

source_lesson.title: Social, Cultural & Economic Factors
source_lesson.description: How relationships, culture, discrimination, employment, and finances affect wellbeing.
source_lesson.content_html:
Social Factors

The people around us have a powerful influence on our health and wellbeing. Social factors include the quality of relationships, whether a person feels included or excluded, and whether they experience bullying or discrimination. These factors can have positive or negative effects across all areas of PIES.

Supportive and Unsupportive Relationships

Supportive relationships with friends, family, peers, and colleagues provide encouragement, practical help, and a sense of belonging. A person who feels supported is more likely to have high self-esteem, manage stress effectively, and maintain good mental health. Family support can encourage healthy eating and exercise, while supportive friendships provide emotional comfort and social opportunities.

Unsupportive relationships have the opposite effect. If a person’s family is critical, neglectful, or abusive, it can lead to low self-esteem, anxiety, depression, and social withdrawal. Unsupportive relationships at work can cause chronic stress, reduced motivation, and difficulty concentrating. Children who grow up without stable, loving relationships may struggle with emotional regulation and forming healthy relationships later in life.

Key Fact

Supportive relationships positively affect all PIES areas: physical (encouragement to stay healthy), intellectual (motivation to learn), emotional (security, self-esteem), social (sense of belonging). Unsupportive relationships have the opposite effect across all areas.

Social Inclusion and Exclusion

Social inclusion means being part of a group or community — feeling accepted and valued. It supports emotional wellbeing by giving a sense of purpose and belonging. Social exclusion means being left out. It can happen because of poverty, disability, language barriers, age, or other factors. Excluded individuals may experience loneliness, depression, and reduced access to services, education, or employment opportunities.

Bullying and Discrimination

Bullying is repeated behaviour intended to hurt, intimidate, or control another person. It can be physical (hitting, pushing), verbal (name-calling, threats), or cyber (online harassment). Bullying severely damages emotional wellbeing, causing anxiety, depression, low self-esteem, and in extreme cases, self-harm. It affects intellectual development through reduced concentration and school avoidance, and social development through isolation and fear of others.

Discrimination means treating someone unfairly because of a characteristic such as age, disability, race, gender, religion, or sexual orientation. It is protected against by the Equality Act 2010. Discrimination in the workplace can limit career progression and income. In healthcare, it can prevent people from accessing the services they need. Experiencing discrimination damages self-esteem, creates stress, and can lead to social withdrawal and poorer health outcomes.

Cultural Factors

Cultural factors relate to the beliefs, values, and practices of the communities people belong to. They shape behaviours and attitudes that can positively or negatively affect health and wellbeing.

Religion: Religious belief can provide a strong sense of community, moral guidance, and emotional support through prayer, worship, and fellowship. However, some religious practices may restrict access to certain medical treatments (e.g. blood transfusions) or create conflict if an individual’s beliefs differ from their family or community.

Gender roles and expectations: Traditional gender roles may limit opportunities — for example, expecting women to be primary carers can restrict career progression and financial independence. Pressure on men to be “strong” and not show emotion can prevent them from seeking help for mental health problems.

Gender identity: An individual whose gender identity does not match the sex they were assigned at birth may face discrimination, bullying, or rejection from family and peers. This can severely affect emotional wellbeing and mental health. Acceptance and support have the opposite, positive effect.

Sexual orientation: Individuals who identify as LGBTQ+ may experience discrimination, prejudice, or bullying, which negatively affects emotional and social wellbeing. In supportive environments, being able to express one’s identity freely has a positive effect on self-esteem and social inclusion.

Community participation: Being involved in community activities (volunteering, clubs, religious groups, sports teams) provides social connections, a sense of purpose, and opportunities for physical activity. It can improve all areas of PIES. Lack of community participation can lead to isolation and loneliness.

Economic Factors

Economic factors relate to money, employment, and financial resources. They have a significant impact on an individual’s ability to access the things needed for good health and wellbeing.

Employment situation: Having a job provides income, routine, social interaction, and a sense of purpose. These positively affect all PIES areas. Unemployment can lead to financial hardship, loss of routine, reduced social contact, low self-esteem, stress, and depression. Long-term unemployment is strongly linked to poor mental and physical health.

Financial resources: These include income (from employment), inheritance, and savings. Having adequate financial resources allows a person to afford nutritious food, suitable housing, heating, healthcare, and leisure activities. Poverty restricts access to all of these, increasing the risk of poor diet, cold or damp housing, stress, and social exclusion. Research consistently shows that people living in poverty have poorer health outcomes and shorter life expectancy than those who are financially secure.

Key Fact

Economic factors underpin many other factors. Poverty can lead to poor nutrition, inadequate housing, limited access to healthcare, and chronic stress — affecting all areas of PIES development.
source_lesson.exam_tip_html: For higher-mark questions on social, cultural, and economic factors, show how factors link together. For example, discrimination (social) may lead to unemployment (economic), which causes poverty (economic), leading to poor housing (environmental) and poor diet (lifestyle). The best answers create chains of cause and effect rather than listing isolated points.
source_lesson.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Social factors (relationships, inclusion/exclusion, bullying, discrimination) directly affect emotional and social wellbeing but also impact physical and intellectual health.
  • Cultural factors (religion, gender roles, gender identity, sexual orientation, community participation) shape behaviours and experiences that can support or hinder wellbeing.
  • Economic factors (employment, income, savings) underpin many other factors — poverty restricts access to nutrition, housing, healthcare, and social opportunities.

practice_questions.text: Identify one social factor that can affect an individual's health and wellbeing.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark(s) for one correct identification:
• Supportive/unsupportive relationships (1)
• Social inclusion/exclusion (1)
• Bullying (1)
• Discrimination (1).

practice_questions.text: Give two ways that supportive relationships can have a positive effect on an individual's health and wellbeing.
practice_questions.marks:
1 marks for each correct way (max 2):
• Encouragement to stay healthy/exercise/eat well (1)
• Emotional comfort/support when stressed (1)
• Increased self-esteem/confidence (1)
• Sense of belonging/reduced loneliness (1)
• Practical help with daily tasks (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain how discrimination can have a negative effect on an individual's emotional and intellectual wellbeing.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks for developed explanation:
• Emotionally, discrimination damages self-esteem (1) because the individual feels unfairly treated and undervalued, leading to anxiety and depression (1).
• Intellectually, discrimination can limit educational or career opportunities (1) because the individual may be denied access to training, promotions, or education, reducing their ability to develop skills and knowledge (1).
• Accept other valid chains of reasoning.

practice_questions.text: Discuss the impact of economic factors on an individual's health and wellbeing.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (5-6): Detailed discussion covering multiple PIES areas with developed points.
Mid band (3-4): Some discussion with partial development.
Lower band (1-2): Limited points with little development.
Indicative content:
• Employment provides income, routine, social interaction, and purpose — all positive for PIES
• Unemployment leads to financial hardship, loss of routine, isolation, low self-esteem
• Adequate income allows access to nutritious food, suitable housing, leisure activities
• Poverty restricts all of these, increasing risk of poor diet, cold/damp housing, stress
• Links between economic factors and other factors: poverty leads to poor nutrition and housing.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the extent to which social factors have a greater impact on an individual's health and wellbeing than economic factors.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (7-8): Comprehensive evaluation with balanced argument and justified conclusion.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Good evaluation with some balance.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Some evaluation with limited balance.
Lower band (1-2): Limited evaluation.
Indicative content:
Social factors:
• Bullying can cause severe emotional damage, self-harm, depression
• Discrimination affects career opportunities and self-worth
• Unsupportive relationships damage emotional security and mental health
• Social exclusion leads to loneliness and isolation
Economic factors:
• Poverty affects access to basic needs — food, housing, heating, healthcare
• Unemployment removes income, routine, and purpose
• Financial stress is a major cause of mental health problems
• Economic factors underpin many social factors — poverty can lead to exclusion
Conclusion: Both are significant. Economic factors may be seen as more fundamental because they affect access to basic needs, but social factors like bullying and discrimination can devastate wellbeing regardless of wealth. The impact depends on the individual's circumstances and resilience.

practice_questions.text: Jamal is 30 years old. He recently lost his job and is struggling to pay rent. He has become isolated from friends and feels embarrassed about his situation. His family live far away and he does not feel supported. He has also experienced racial discrimination when applying for new jobs. Using the case study, assess how social and economic factors are affecting Jamal's overall health and wellbeing.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (8-10): Comprehensive response covering all PIES areas with clear links to Jamal's circumstances.
Upper-mid band (5-7): Good coverage of multiple PIES areas with some links.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Some relevant points but limited development.
Lower band (1-2): Basic points with little reference to the case study.
Indicative content:
• Physical: Financial hardship may mean Jamal cannot afford nutritious food or heating, affecting physical health. Stress from job loss can cause headaches, sleep problems, weakened immune system.
• Intellectual: Without work, Jamal loses mental stimulation and routine. Discrimination may prevent him from accessing employment that uses his skills.
• Emotional: Job loss causes low self-esteem and embarrassment. Isolation from friends reduces emotional support. Racial discrimination damages self-worth and causes anger/frustration. Lack of family support leaves him without a safety net.
• Social: Isolation from friends means reduced social interaction. Embarrassment prevents him from reaching out. Distance from family reduces practical and emotional support. Discrimination excludes him from the job market.
• Links: Economic factors (job loss) lead to social factors (isolation, embarrassment). Discrimination (social/cultural) creates barriers to resolving economic problems (employment). These factors compound each other in a negative cycle.
• Synoptic: Jamal is in early adulthood — typically a time of career building and relationship formation. These life events disrupt expected development (Component 1). Support services could help (Component 2).

glossary_terms.definition: Factors relating to an individual’s relationships and interactions with other people, including family, friends, peers, and colleagues.
Being part of a group or community, feeling accepted and valued by others.
Being left out of a group or community, feeling rejected or isolated from others.
A situation where a person or family lacks the financial resources to meet their basic needs, including food, housing, and heating.
